Elkaffas2 Abstract The rapid digitization of financial transactions has increased efficiency but also exposed systems to sophisticated fraud attempts, posing significant challenges to ensuring transaction security. Traditional fraud detection approaches, including rule‑based systems and conventional machine learning models, struggle to adapt to evolving fraud pat‑ terns, resulting in high false‑positive rates and limited scalability. State‑of‑the‑art methods, while leveraging deep learning, face limitations such as computational overhead, lack of transparency, and vulnerability to adversarial attacks. This study explores the integration of lightweight blockchain technology and deep learning for robust fraud detection in financial transactions. Lightweight blockchain ensures transaction immutability, transparency, and tam‑ per‑proof data sharing across nodes, addressing trust and security challenges. Meanwhile, deep learning provides dynamic and adaptive detection capabilities, employing neural networks to identify anomalous patterns in complex datasets. By reducing the computational and storage demands of traditional blockchain systems, the lightweight approach facilitates real‑time fraud detection in resource‑constrained environments, such as mobile and IoT devices. Our model combines these components, ensuring data integrity through blockchain while enabling efficient pattern recognition via deep learning, creating a system capable of addressing scalability, energy efficiency, and adaptability. Preliminary experiments demonstrate the model’s effectiveness in reducing false positives, enhancing detection rates, and achieving scalability without compromising security or performance, marking a significant step toward secure and efficient financial ecosystems. JSON: Name: lightweight_blockchain_mobilenet_fraud Title: Lightweight blockchain‐enabled MobileNet‐LSTM framework for real‐time fraud detection in financial transaction systems Short Hypothesis: Integrating a permissioned lightweight blockchain for immutable logging and verification with a MobileNet‐based lightweight CNN feeding an LSTM temporal module will reduce false positive rate and end‐to‐end detection latency for real‐time financial transaction fraud detection compared to equivalent detection models without blockchain logging. Related Work: Prior work divides into three lines: (1) conventional ML and deep learning for fraud detection (decision trees, SVM, RandomForest, LSTM, CNN, Transformer) which achieve high accuracy but often require large models, heavy compute, and are vulnerable to concept drift and adversarial examples; (2) lightweight deep architectures (MobileNet, SqueezeNet, EfficientNet) and model compression (pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation) that trade marginal accuracy for much lower inference cost, making edge deployment feasible; (3) blockchain and permissioned ledgers (Hyperledger, PoS, PoA) and cryptographic primitives (Merkle trees, ZKPs) applied to financial integrity, privacy, and decentralized audit, but suffering from storage, latency, and privacy exposure when used naively. Existing hybrid attempts either embed heavyweight models on-chain or use blockchain only for data provenance; unresolved issues include combined optimization of model footprint and chain overhead, real‐time verification latency, privacy leakage from on‐chain metadata, and empirical robustness against adversarial transaction perturbations. Abstract: We address secure, real‐time fraud detection for financial transactions by combining a lightweight blockchain layer for immutable logging and verification with a compressed deep learning detector tailored for edge environments. The proposed high‐level approach uses MobileNet‐style depthwise‐separable convolutions to extract compact spatial features from temporally encoded transaction windows and an LSTM (or attention) module to capture sequential patterns; transaction metadata and prediction proofs are recorded on a permissioned lightweight blockchain using compact Merkle proofs and optional zero‐knowledge proofs for privacy. The main contribution is a co‐designed pipeline that jointly optimizes model footprint, inference latency, and blockchain verification overhead to enable deployment on mobile and IoT endpoints while preserving auditable integrity and selective privacy. Expected outcomes are measurable reductions in false positive rate and end‐to‐end detection latency versus non‐integrated baselines, demonstrable tamper detection, and quantified privacy leakage reduction when ZKPs are applied. Experiments: Datasets: IEEE‐CIS Fraud Detection (real credit card), European Credit Card Fraud (anonymized), PaySim Mobile Transaction (simulated mobile), Synthetic custom dataset (controlled fraud ratio 10%). Data splits: 80/20 train/test, stratified; 5‐fold cross‐validation on training set for hyperparameter selection. Baselines: rule‐based system; RandomForest; SVM; LSTM; CNN; Transformer; MobileNet‐only (no recurrent layer); MobileNet+LSTM (no blockchain); blockchain‐only logging with basic threshold detector. Metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, False Positive Rate (FPR), AUC‐ROC, inference latency per transaction (ms), CPU% and RAM (MB) during inference, throughput (TPS), blockchain latency (ms), blockchain storage footprint (MB per 1k txns), tamper detection rate (%), Information Gain, Mutual Information, Membership Inference Attack accuracy. Experimental setup: development on machine with Intel i7 CPU, NVIDIA RTX 3050 Ti, 16GB RAM; edge targets: representative smartphone (Android, 8‐core, 4GB RAM) and Raspberry Pi 4 (4GB RAM). Training: Adam optimizer, lr=5e‐4, batch=128, epochs=50; MobileNet width/resolution multipliers swept {0.5,1.0}. Blockchain: Hyperledger Fabric simulation for permissioned PoS; Merkle proofs for per‐prediction logging; optional ZK‐SNARK (Circom/SnarkJS) circuits for proof of model output conformance. Comparative/ablation studies: (A) MobileNet+LSTM vs LSTM/CNN/Transformer; (B) MobileNet+LSTM with vs without blockchain logging; (C) blockchain with vs without ZKPs (measure IG/MI/MIA); (D) compressed MobileNet variants (pruning/quantization) vs full MobileNet; (E) adversarial robustness: train GAN to generate adversarial transactions, evaluate drop in detection metrics and adversarial detection rate. Deployment tests: measure inference latency, CPU/RAM, and throughput on cloud, mobile, and IoT targets; measure end‐to‐end detection+verification latency with blockchain under different block sizes and batching strategies. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: adversarially crafted transactions may bypass detector and also manipulate logged metadata; ZK‐SNARK proving time may be nontrivial off‐chain and verification gas cost may be prohibitive for frequent per‐transaction proofs. Data and evaluation biases: public datasets are imbalanced and may not reflect all real fraud modalities; synthetic datasets risk overfitting to simulated patterns and inflated performance. Scalability and compute limits: combined system requires both inference compute and blockchain validation resources; edge devices with very low RAM/CPU may exhibit unacceptable latency or accuracy loss. Storage and network constraints: blockchain storage grows with logged metadata; bandwidth limitations increase verification latency. Generalization limits: models trained on card/mobile datasets may not generalize across geographies, payment rails, or novel fraud tactics; permissioned blockchain assumptions (trusted validators) limit applicability to fully decentralized settings.
